page.title: Improving Golf Swing Pose Estimation
page.description: Bringing golf swing pose estimation closer to practical use through targeted dataset expansion and an efficient annotation workflow.
page.role: My role: I led annotation operations, developed the training and Core ML conversion pipeline, and collaborated with the iOS team on deployment.

sections.title: Abstract
paragraphs: Golf-specific postures and arm occlusions exposed weaknesses in general-purpose pose estimation. I led a targeted annotation effort that reduced labeling workload by approximately two-thirds and increased labeling speed by approximately 3×, delivering 30,000 annotated frames in two weeks for around US$3,000. The resulting lightweight model resolved approximately 80% of the previously difficult examples assessed, suggesting that better data coverage could improve accuracy without a larger architecture.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: General-purpose pose models can perform well on everyday movements yet struggle with golf swings. Unusual joint configurations, rapid motion, and arms occluded by the torso can produce anatomically implausible predictions at positions important to swing analysis.

We suspected that insufficient coverage of these poses in the training data was a major contributor. However, exhaustively labeling hundreds of videos, each containing hundreds of frames, was impractical under the available time and budget.
The central question was: Could targeted data selection and a more efficient annotation process improve difficult-pose estimation while retaining a lightweight model?

sections.title: Methods

subsections.title: Prioritize useful footage
paragraphs: The first challenge was controlling annotation volume. I worked with the team to define more objective video-selection criteria, focusing the effort on footage relevant to the observed prediction failures. This reduced the annotation workload by approximately two-thirds.

subsections.title: Make joint definitions actionable
paragraphs: Annotators needed to make consistent decisions in ambiguous or occluded poses. I refined several joint definitions and documented their rationale, alongside practical labeling techniques. These changes reduced ambiguity and helped increase labeling speed to approximately 3× its previous rate.

subsections.title: Coordinate annotation delivery
paragraphs: I managed an outsourced annotation team of around 10 people, using the internal management tool to coordinate the work. The team delivered approximately 480,000 joint annotations across 30,000 frames in about two weeks, at a cost of around US$3,000.

subsections.title: Connect annotation to model iteration
paragraphs: I established a data-preparation pipeline to combine existing and newly annotated datasets, followed by model training, inference, Core ML conversion, and quantization. Working with the iOS team, I carried the resulting model through to deployment on iPhones.

sections.note: Proprietary selection criteria, training settings, and internal tooling details are omitted.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: The golf-specific model produced more plausible estimates in the difficult cases assessed, particularly when the torso occluded the arms. Approximately 80% of the previously difficult examples were resolved, while inference remained near YOLO-nano speed.

The model was developed during the YOLOv8 era. In the examples shown, it achieves accuracy similar to YOLO26x on visible joints while remaining more reliable during down-the-line follow-throughs and face-on transitions. It also suppresses non-golfer pose distractions and remains lightweight enough for real-time inference on iPhones.

subsections.title: Data coverage was a practical bottleneck
paragraphs: The results support the hypothesis that insufficient training-data coverage contributed substantially to the observed failures. A lightweight model could learn more plausible predictions for difficult golf poses after targeted dataset expansion, without requiring a larger architecture.

The examples also show plausible predictions under occlusion or blur using individual frames, without information from preceding or following frames. This suggests that useful visual cues remained available even when individual joints were difficult to see directly.

subsections.title: Annotation efficiency enabled model improvement
paragraphs: The contribution was not simply adding more labels. Reducing unnecessary work, clarifying annotation decisions, and improving labeling speed made dataset expansion feasible within the available constraints.
The model outcome and annotation process should therefore be evaluated together: prediction quality was the final objective, while annotation efficiency made that improvement achievable.

subsections.title: A repeatable path from data to deployment
paragraphs: From an MLOps perspective, the project established a reusable path from dataset preparation through training and mobile deployment. Documented joint definitions and annotation workflows also gave later annotation rounds a starting point.
This foundation supports future model iterations with less repeated setup work. Further automation of dataset checks, evaluation, and deployment verification would strengthen the process.

subsections.title: Future directions
paragraphs: A next step would be a repeatable cycle of failure collection, targeted annotation, retraining, and held-out evaluation. The same approach could be explored in other sports, animation, entertainment, or medical applications, but each domain would require its own data and validation.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: Targeted annotation improved difficult golf-pose estimation while preserving a lightweight, real-time model. By reducing annotation volume and making labeling faster and less ambiguous, I helped turn a costly dataset-expansion problem into a feasible model-improvement cycle. The resulting workflow provides a foundation for continued data-driven iteration.
